overview: Black answers 1.c4 with ...g6 and, after 2.e4, strikes back with ...e5. The position resembles a reversed Sicilian-style Maroczy with a fianchetto bishop. White usually continues Nc3 and g3 or d4 with a lead in space.

white_ideas.idea: Develop Nc3, g3 and Bg2 and keep the centre under control
Take space with d3/f4 or play d4 to open lines

typical_structures.structure: Symmetrical e4/e5 with c4 against g6
Open centre if White plays d4

character.notes: Not forcing; both sides develop with chances.

soundness.notes: Adorjan's idea is accepted as playable; neither side stands badly.

structure.notes: Flexible; 3.d4 exd4 opens the centre but quieter lines keep it tense.

approach.notes: Named after Adorjan but not seriously rare, so standard.

level.notes: Plans of a mixed structure but not demanding.

sublines_that_differ.name: 3.d4
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. c4 g6 2. e4 e5 3. d4 exd4 4. Qxd4 Nf6
sublines_that_differ.how: White opens the centre for an Open Sicilian-like game.

character.reason: The play is positional with chances for both and little forcing theory.

structure.reason: The centre stays tense between e4/e5 and the c4 pawn.

approach.reason: It is a normal if uncommon way to meet 1.c4 played by good players.

level.reason: Positional plans are needed but there is little to memorise.

plans.reason: The g7 and g2 bishops and the d5 square set the character.
